seed_situation: At a community dental practice, a dental assistant with no authority over the rota asks the front-desk receptionist, who also cannot approve shift swaps, whether a hygienist's request to swap two shifts next week is for a health reason and whether it is serious enough to affect the afternoon clinic. The receptionist knows the answer is a minor wrist strain, but only because the hygienist mentioned it quietly after an appointment and asked that it not be passed on. The receptionist wants to give a straight answer so the schedule can be adjusted, but feels uneasy about repeating the detail.
why_it_is_hard: A direct answer would help the coworker make sense of the rota, but it would also pass on a small private health detail shared in confidence. The pull is between being useful to the practice and not exposing what the hygienist asked to keep quiet.
varied_fact: the confidential health detail is a minor wrist strain rather than a serious, potentially career-affecting health condition

situation_features.relationship: coworkers in a dental practice; one has been told a colleague's private health information
situation_features.note: both questioner and respondent lack authority over the rota; the information was shared privately and there is no emergency

seed_situation: A district nursing team visits the asker's mother each morning to give eye drops and check a mild leg ulcer. The asker's sister, a nurse on the same team, privately admits that she has been logging visits as on time while shifting them later to manage childcare, so several housebound patients receive drops and dressings an hour or two late and feel irritation; she asks the asker not to say anything because an audit could cost her job and change the mother's familiar nurse. The team covers about forty patients, and the asker believes a complaint would quickly force a schedule review and reduce the delays for many of them. The new rota begins in three days, and the asker, who has no role on the team, has drafted an anonymous message pretending to be a neighbour who has tracked the late arrivals; she wants permission to send it.
why_it_is_hard: Keeping the sister's confidence protects a family member and preserves the mother's familiar care, but it leaves other patients absorbing repeated minor delays; sending the invented complaint would likely trigger a schedule review for many patients, yet it would rely on falsehood and damage the sister. The asker also has to decide how long she can remain silent while her own mother benefits from the schedule the sister has falsified.

situation_features.relationship: adult sisters, one a district nurse, the other the daughter caring for their mother
situation_features.note: the asker has no authority on the nursing team; the proposed action is an invented anonymous complaint; the mother benefits from the current schedule

seed_situation: At an ambulance dispatch centre, a call-taker left her console for ten minutes to settle her frightened teenage son, who had come to reception with a minor cut, while a non-emergency transport request waited in the queue. Before stepping away she put the request into a hidden holding status so it would not alert the backup team; the caller eventually got a ride but missed a pharmacy pickup and waited outside in the rain, and the call-taker says the delay was only a side effect of calming her son. A fellow call-taker, with no supervisory power, is angry and wants to force a finding of misconduct in the semi-public staff channel before the shift review ends.
why_it_is_hard: The child's immediate claim and the stranger's claim to the service both press at once, and giving full attention to either leaves the other with a real loss. It is also unclear whether the caller's delay was merely accepted while she helped her son or was part of the method that kept the console free, and how blameworthy she is under panic and competing duties cannot be settled by the queue log.

situation_features.relationship: call-taker and fellow call-taker; the call-taker is the mother of the teenage boy; the delayed caller is a stranger
situation_features.note: semi-public staff channel; non-emergency queue; the act/blame split and the side-effect-versus-method question are both live

seed_situation: I work as a pharmacy assistant in a hospital pharmacy. A close colleague, who trained me and shares my shift, has been using the department's small consumables account to order pricey hand creams, vitamins, and specialty snacks, labeling them as staff-welfare items; the orders show up in a shared supply log that several of us can see. I have also used some of the snacks, and when I asked her about it she said it is just a perk and management won't miss the amount. I don't want to get her in trouble or look like I'm attacking her, but the log makes me worry that I'll be seen as part of it.
why_it_is_hard: Closeness and shared benefit pull toward keeping quiet, while the shared log and department funds mean the asker may owe a correction or report; reporting a small, non-urgent misuse could damage the colleague's standing and the relationship, but staying silent may leave the asker involved and let a small loss continue.

situation_features.relationship: close colleague and trainer on the same pharmacy shift
situation_features.note: the asker has also benefited from the purchases and is defensive about not being blamed

seed_situation: I volunteer as a craft helper at a public residential dementia unit, with no supervisory role. During a common-room session open to residents and visiting relatives, one resident took another resident's labelled cardigan, wore it, and stained it with paint. The owner's daughter has asked me directly which resident did it and wants the matter recorded before Friday's family meeting. The resident who took it is distressed, has dementia, and may face tighter restrictions if the complaint names her; I need a quick, practical answer about what to tell the daughter.
why_it_is_hard: The daughter has a real claim to an honest account and repair for her mother's damaged clothing, while the resident who caused the damage has dementia and is already suffering distress. Naming her may satisfy the request but expose her to penalties beyond a minor harm; refusing details may protect her but leave the owner's family without what they are owed.

situation_features.relationship: volunteer craft helper and a resident's daughter
situation_features.note: Minor property damage occurred in a public common-room setting; the asker has no formal authority and wants a fast way to close the complaint.

seed_situation: A junior communications assistant at a fertility clinic monitors the clinic's public livestreams and patient Q&A chat, but has no power to override the platform's automated moderation tool. During an earlier public session, a former patient mocked the assistant's speech and posted a false claim that the clinic's automated reminder texts carried a hidden fee, causing only brief confusion and no clinical harm. The tool suspended the account. Now, minutes before tonight's livestream, the former patient sends a short apology and asks to rejoin the public chat, and the assistant, wanting to accept the apology but uneasy about reopening the forum, is asked by the manager for a recommendation while the automated appeal waits in a human-review queue.
why_it_is_hard: Forgiving the personal insult pulls toward accepting the apology and restoring access, while protecting the public patient space and the assistant's own ability to do the job pulls toward keeping the suspension until there is clear evidence of changed behaviour; either route can either treat a minor lapse as unforgivable or leave the forum exposed to repeat disruption.

situation_features.relationship: junior communications assistant, manager, and a former patient in a public clinic chat
situation_features.note: Automated moderation suspension with a human-review appeal; personal insult and minor public misinformation, no clinical decision involved.

seed_situation: A part-time literacy tutor at a further education college, with no welfare role, has access to a small student pantry stocked for enrolled learners who miss meals between classes. One evening, after the welfare office has closed and nothing else on campus is open, a teenager from the neighbourhood who is not a student asks privately for something to eat before a long bus ride home. The tutor gives them two sandwiches from the pantry without formal permission and feels torn between the learners they teach and the unknown young person. There is no current emergency, the loss is minor, and the question is whether to continue such informal help, replace the food quietly, or direct future requests to the welfare office.
why_it_is_hard: Direct, local help can meet a real need without delay, but it uses food set aside for enrolled learners and bypasses the college's central welfare service, which may have better resources and more consistent rules. If the tutor stops, an unknown young person may go hungry; if the tutor continues, the learners and the welfare service may carry the cost of an arrangement they did not agree to.

situation_features.relationship: part-time tutor, enrolled learners, and an unknown neighbourhood teenager
situation_features.note: small private use of a student pantry; no formal authority; no ongoing emergency; conflict between personal aid and central support
